did_you_know.text: The title identifies the psalm as a “maskil of David” and notes that it was sung “according to Mahalath.” The verse itself suggests that it is a thoughtful or instructive psalm.
The psalm portrays the fool as someone who says in his heart, “There is no God.” According to the rest of the verse, this inward denial is connected with moral corruption and wrongdoing.
The verse presents God as looking down from heaven on humanity and examining whether there is anyone with understanding—someone who seeks and pursues God.
The psalm’s description of the human condition is extremely bleak: “All have turned away; together they have become corrupt.” It goes on to say that there is not even one person who does good.

The evildoers are described as “those who devour my people,” a vivid expression emphasizing the severity of the harm they inflict and the cruelty with which they treat them. The verse adds that they do not call on God.
The psalm distinguishes between real fear and baseless fear: the wicked spread terror, but in the end God scatters their camp, puts them to shame, and rejects them.
The phrase “he scattered the bones of those who besieged you” describes the defeat of the wicked in vivid and forceful language, emphasizing the collapse of the enemy’s power.
The psalm concludes with a prayer for Israel’s salvation from Zion and for the restoration of the people. The hoped-for result of redemption is twofold joy: “Let Jacob rejoice; let Israel be glad.”
